clinicalPearls: The leading cause of fatal mushroom poisoning worldwide, most often from Amanita phalloides (death cap) and certain Galerina and Lepiota species that contain cyclopeptide amatoxins.

Classically follows a triphasic course: a symptom-free latent period, a severe gastrointestinal (cholera-like) phase, and a hepatorenal phase with rising transaminases and possible fulminant hepatic failure.
A characteristically long latent interval before the onset of vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea is an important clue distinguishing it from early-onset, more benign mushroom toxins.

Alpha-amanitin inhibits RNA polymerase II, halting messenger RNA and protein synthesis, with hepatocytes and renal tubular cells most affected because of enterohepatic recirculation and renal excretion.
A deceptive phase of apparent clinical improvement often follows the gastrointestinal illness just as hepatic necrosis is accelerating, and can lull clinicians into false reassurance.
Amatoxins are heat-stable and not destroyed by cooking, drying or freezing, and there is no reliable taste or odour warning.

Management centres on aggressive fluid resuscitation, activated charcoal, interruption of enterohepatic circulation, and agents such as intravenous silibinin and high-dose penicillin, with N-acetylcysteine used as in other causes of hepatic failure; liver transplantation may be life-saving.
Early referral to a liver transplant centre and use of prognostic criteria for hepatic failure are essential once coagulopathy or encephalopathy appears.
reference.pathophysiology: Amatoxin poisoning is caused by bicyclic octapeptide toxins, principally alpha-amanitin, found in Amanita phalloides and related Galerina and Lepiota species. After ingestion the toxin is absorbed from the gut and taken up into hepatocytes by the organic anion transporting polypeptide system, undergoing extensive enterohepatic recirculation that prolongs hepatic exposure. Within the cell alpha-amanitin binds tightly to RNA polymerase II, blocking transcription of messenger RNA; the resulting arrest of protein synthesis leads to cell death, most severely in tissues with high metabolic and synthetic turnover such as the hepatocytes lining the periportal and centrilobular zones, gastrointestinal mucosa and renal proximal tubular cells. The gastrointestinal epithelial injury produces the profuse secretory diarrhoea and vomiting of the second phase, while progressive hepatocellular necrosis over subsequent days manifests as steeply rising aminotransferases, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy that may culminate in fulminant hepatic failure. Direct tubular toxicity and hypovolaemic prerenal injury combine to cause acute kidney injury. The toxin is excreted in urine and bile, and its heat stability means ordinary cooking offers no protection.
additionalDifferentials: Early-onset gastrointestinal mushroom toxins (e.g. gastrointestinal irritant species) with benign course
Orellanine-containing mushroom poisoning causing delayed nephrotoxicity
Paracetamol or other drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure
Other causes of acute liver failure such as Wilson disease or autoimmune hepatitis
additionalInvestigations: Serial liver function tests including aminotransferases and bilirubin to track hepatic injury
Coagulation profile (prothrombin time or INR) as a key marker of hepatic synthetic failure and prognosis
Blood glucose monitoring for hypoglycaemia from hepatic failure
Renal function and electrolytes for concurrent acute kidney injury
Serum lactate and arterial blood gas in severe or deteriorating cases
Detection of amatoxin in urine or gastric aspirate at a reference laboratory where available
Mycological identification of ingested or vomited mushroom material and spore examination
redFlags: Gastrointestinal symptoms beginning only after a prolonged latent interval following a mushroom meal
Rising transaminases or prothrombin time after apparent recovery from the gastrointestinal phase
Any feature of hepatic encephalopathy such as confusion or asterixis
Oliguria or rising creatinine indicating acute kidney injury
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the amount ingested and the speed of treatment; with modern intensive care and antidotal therapy many patients survive, but those developing progressive coagulopathy, encephalopathy or hypoglycaemia have a high mortality without liver transplantation. Early recognition and referral to a transplant centre markedly improve survival.
pitfalls: False reassurance during the deceptive phase of improvement while hepatic necrosis is advancing
Discharging a patient whose gastrointestinal symptoms settle without arranging serial liver and coagulation monitoring
Assuming cooking or drying detoxifies the mushrooms, as amatoxins are heat-stable
Delaying contact with a liver transplant centre until fulminant failure is established
Attributing the initial illness to simple gastroenteritis and overlooking the long latent period
references: Hepatology and acute liver failure guidelines
Mushroom poisoning and poisons-centre reference materials
management: Resuscitate with intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacement to counter the cholera-like gastrointestinal losses and preserve renal perfusion
Interrupt enterohepatic recirculation with multiple-dose activated charcoal
Give hepatoprotective antidotes, intravenous silibinin and N-acetylcysteine, as early as possible
Monitor liver function, prothrombin time or INR, glucose and renal function serially, correcting hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy
Refer promptly to specialist hepatology and a liver transplant centre, using prognostic criteria to identify need for transplantation
Support failing organs in critical care, including renal replacement therapy and management of hepatic encephalopathy
Confirm the toxin by amatoxin assay of urine or gastric aspirate where available and involve poisons information services
